title: Rejected: How Modern Art Began
description: The Salon des Refusés, Impressionism's insulting name, and why 'unfinished' once meant 'not art'

concepts.title: The Salon and the Salon of the Rejected
concepts.contentHtml:
Start with a simple question: in 1860s Paris, who decided what counted as art? A jury did. The Salon was the official, and for many years the only, exhibition for artists' work in Paris, and success there was of the greatest importance for a painter's career. Collectors often would not buy a picture the jury had refused, and some demanded refunds if a work they had bought was later rejected.

The jury of 1863 was exceptionally harsh. It accepted works from only one-third of the artists who applied, and more than half of the five thousand works presented were turned away.1 The uproar reached Emperor Napoleon III, who ordered the refused works to be shown in an exhibition of their own, next to the official Salon, so that the public could judge for themselves. Here is the surprise: the most famous show of rejected art in history was created by an emperor, who probably cared less about painting than about making his regime look tolerant.2

The Salon des Refusés opened on 15 May 1863. More than six hundred artists withdrew rather than risk the stigma, and the hasty catalogue listed only 781 of an estimated 1,500 works. Crowds came anyway, as many as four thousand on free Sundays, and many came to laugh. Not every rejected picture was a hidden masterpiece; plenty were mediocre.

The star of the scandal was Édouard Manet's Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe (Luncheon on the Grass), a large canvas now in the Musée d'Orsay in Paris. In a wood, beside the remains of a picnic, two young men in city clothes sit talking on the grass. Behind them a woman in her shift bathes in a pond. In front, a second woman sits on a blue cloth, entirely naked, her fashionable clothes piled in the foreground, and she looks straight out of the picture at you. Manet borrowed the arrangement from Renaissance works, yet critics attacked his drawing, composition and handling of paint even more than the nudity.

concepts.title: A Sneer That Named a Movement
concepts.contentHtml:
Eleven years later, a group of painters stopped waiting for the jury. In April 1874 thirty artists, among them Claude Monet, Auguste Renoir, Edgar Degas, Berthe Morisot, Camille Pissarro and Paul Cézanne, opened their own exhibition in Paris, independent of the official Salon. The work shown was greeted with derision, and one picture was singled out for ridicule: Monet's Impression, Sunrise.

Picture the harbour of Le Havre through morning mist, seen from a hotel window. The sky and water are a muted, misty grey; ships and smoke plumes are quick, blurred marks; and a vibrant orange sun hangs low, its reflection broken into a few short orange strokes on the water. The painting is now in the Musée Marmottan Monet in Paris. The critic Louis Leroy, writing in the satirical paper Le Charivari, seized on its title and mocked the whole group as "Impressionists", commenting that the painting was less finished than "wallpaper in its embryonic state".1 The insult stuck and became the movement's name. The group held seven further exhibitions until 1886.

The picture kept one more secret. The Texas State University astronomer Donald Olson set out to find exactly when Monet painted it. He used old photographs of Le Havre to reconstruct the view from Monet's hotel room. The height of the sun suggested about 20 to 30 minutes after sunrise.2 Large sailing ships could enter the shallow harbour only at high tide, which left 19 possible dates. Weather records and the direction of the smoke narrowed these to two. The art historian Géraldine Lefebvre argued for 1872, matching the "72" beside Monet's signature, which gave 13 November 1872 at about 7:35 in the morning. The findings appeared in a 2014 exhibition catalogue.

Notice two things. First, the date is only as good as one assumption: that Monet recorded the time of day faithfully. Second, the work settled an older argument, because some art historians had even contended that the painting shows a sunset.3 Science cannot tell you whether a picture is art, but it can test what a picture shows.

concepts.title: Why 'Unfinished' Meant 'Not Art'
concepts.contentHtml:
Why did educated Parisians find these pictures so wrong? Mostly not because of their subjects. The Academy ranked history painting, biblical, mythological or political scenes, at the top, and its juries expected high moral themes and an exquisite, perfected finish: smooth surfaces in which the brushstrokes disappear. They disapproved of contemporary subjects and of loose, sketchy brushwork.1 A canvas that showed its brushmarks looked to them like a sketch someone had forgotten to complete.

The Impressionists broke that rule on purpose. Instead of working up a picture in the studio from sketches, they painted out of doors, quickly, in front of the subject, to catch the momentary and transient effects of sunlight. Their brushwork became rapid and broken into separate dabs in order to render the fleeting quality of light.2 They also took full advantage of new, factory-made artists' materials, a story the pigments topic tells. What critics called carelessness was a method.

One reaction shows how strange this looked, even to a future revolutionary. In Moscow in the mid-1890s a young lawyer named Vasily Kandinsky saw one of Monet's Haystacks. "That it was a haystack the catalogue informed me," he later wrote. "I could not recognize it." He felt the painter had no right to paint so indistinctly, and yet the picture gripped him and lodged in his memory.3 Soon afterwards he gave up law for painting; lesson 3 follows where that led.

This is the pattern the rest of this topic keeps meeting. Every age has unwritten rules for what art must look like, and the rules feel like nature until someone breaks them. In 1874 the broken rule was finish. Within a generation, independent artists, dealers and exhibitions had broken the official Salon's power, and the next rebels would ask a bolder question: does a picture have to look like anything at all?

title: Breaking the Window: Cubism
description: How Cézanne, Picasso and Braque abandoned the single viewpoint and glued the real world into pictures

concepts.title: The Window That Cracked
concepts.contentHtml:
From the Renaissance onwards, European painters treated a picture as a window. Using linear perspective, they built the illusion of real, deep space seen from one fixed viewpoint, as if you stood on a single spot and looked through the frame. (The topic on how to look at a picture explains perspective itself.) Everything in the picture obeyed that one eye.

By the late nineteenth century some painters were growing tired of the window. In 1890 the French painter and writer Maurice Denis published a sentence that became one of the most quoted in modern art: "Remember, that a picture, before it is a picture of a battle horse, a nude woman, or some story, is essentially a flat surface covered in colours arranged in a certain order.1" That is a startling shift. It says the real subject of a painting is the painting itself.

The painter who did most to crack the window was Paul Cézanne, who had shown at the first Impressionist exhibition. In his late work he can be seen painting things from slightly different points of view within one picture, as if he had moved his head while looking.2 Critics who cared most about form, line and colour rather than story, the formalists, took Cézanne as their hero.

Then two younger painters in Paris pushed the idea to its limit. Around 1907–08 Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque began bringing different views of a subject together in the same picture. By breaking objects and figures into distinct flat facets, or planes, they showed several viewpoints at once, and in doing so they stressed the flatness of the canvas instead of creating the illusion of depth. It was a revolutionary break with the tradition of the fixed viewpoint. When Braque's paintings were shown in Paris in 1908, the critic Louis Vauxcelles said they reduced everything to "geometric outlines, to cubes",3 and once again a critic's jibe became a movement's name: Cubism.

concepts.title: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon
concepts.contentHtml:
The painting usually named as the starting gun of Cubism is Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon of 1907. On a canvas nearly eight feet (about 2.4 metres) square, five nude women with distorted anatomy are built from a jarring assemblage of disorderly facets, triangular and rectangular wedges and other geometric shapes.1 There is no rational focus of attention: your eye is forced to look everywhere, as if at pieces of broken glass.

The faces are the shock. Two of the women seem to wear African masks; the other three have eyes on different levels and noses jutting out like pieces of architecture. Picasso was inspired by African masks, which are highly stylised yet present a vivid human image. "A head," he said, "is a matter of eyes, nose, mouth, which can be distributed in any way you like." When he showed the canvas to his friends, their reaction was almost universally negative, and he rolled it up and refused to exhibit it publicly.2 Yet in 2004 a poll of 500 art experts ranked the painting the second most influential work of modern art.3

Now a myth worth busting. People often say Picasso painted like this because he could not paint "properly". The opposite is true. He was the son of an academic painter and studied at the fine arts academy in Barcelona. Early in 1897, aged 15, he began Science and Charity, a large, carefully academic canvas, 197.5 by 250 centimetres, now in the Museu Picasso in Barcelona. In a sickroom scene, a doctor stands for modern medicine and a nun for charity. His father chose the subject to please juries and posed for the doctor, and the picture won one of 125 honourable mentions at the national fine arts exhibition in Madrid that year.4

So Cubism was a choice, not a failure of skill. That matters for this topic's big question: when a highly trained painter deliberately breaks the rules, the breaking itself becomes part of the meaning.

concepts.title: Glue, Rope and Newspaper: Collage
concepts.contentHtml:
Cubism had two phases. Analytical Cubism, from about 1908 to 1912, looks severe: an interweaving of planes and lines in muted blacks, greys and ochres, in which the subject can be hard to find. Synthetic Cubism, from about 1912 to 1914, uses simpler shapes and brighter colours. It also did something new: it stuck pieces of the real world onto the picture, such as scraps of newspaper.

In 1912 Picasso and Braque started to incorporate collage elements into their paintings and to experiment with pasted paper,1 sticking cloth, paper and other materials onto their canvases. Picasso's Still Life with Chair Caning (1912) is a small oval, about 29 by 37 centimetres, painted in oil. Into a Cubist jumble of shapes, lines and letters he glued a piece of printed oilcloth made to look like woven chair caning, a factory-made imitation of a handmade surface, and instead of a frame he edged the oval with thick rope. It is often counted as the first use of collage in fine art.2 The French term papiers collés, for techniques of pasting paper cut-outs onto a surface,3 gave us the word collage.

Why does this matter so much? A painted newspaper is a picture of a newspaper; a pasted newspaper is a newspaper. Once real material entered the picture, the line between showing the world and presenting a piece of it began to blur. Tate calls the inclusion of real objects directly in art the start of one of the most important ideas in modern art.4

Follow that idea one step further and you no longer need the painting at all. You could take a whole manufactured object, put it in an exhibition and call it art. Within five years of the chair caning, someone did, and the object he chose was a urinal.

title: Pictures of Nothing: The Birth of Abstraction
description: Kandinsky, Malevich's Black Square and Hilma af Klint, who got there first and hid it

concepts.title: Kandinsky: Painting Like Music
concepts.contentHtml:
Abstract art does not attempt an accurate depiction of visual reality; it uses shapes, colours, forms and gestural marks to achieve its effect. There are two kinds. Some abstraction simplifies a real object, figure or landscape until it is barely recognisable, as Cubism did. The more radical kind, which some artists called non-objective art, uses forms with no source at all in the visible world. In the decade from about 1910, several painters, mostly working separately, crossed that line.

The most famous was Vasily Kandinsky. He studied law and economics at the University of Moscow and lectured there, but in 1896 he declined a teaching post to study painting in Munich.1 Two experiences, he later wrote, set him on this path. One was Monet's Haystacks, the painting he could not recognise (lesson 1). The other was a performance of Wagner's opera Lohengrin, during which, he wrote, "I saw all my colors in spirit, before my eyes." It became clear to him that painting was capable of developing powers akin to those of music.2

Music was the key. A melody imitates nothing, yet it can move you to tears. Kandinsky wanted colour and line to work the same way, directly on the feelings, without needing a recognisable subject. He set out the argument in his book On the Spiritual in Art, published in December 1911, and soon afterwards he and Franz Marc held the first exhibition of their group Der Blaue Reiter (The Blue Rider) in Munich.

A grim footnote shows how threatening this freedom could seem. In the Nazi purge of "degenerate art" in 1937, fifty-seven of Kandinsky's works were confiscated.3 Like Impressionism before it, abstraction provoked not only puzzlement but power.

Was Kandinsky the first abstract painter? He is generally regarded as the pioneer of abstract art, but the next two concepts show why "first" is a slippery word.

concepts.title: Black Square: The Zero of Painting
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1915, at an exhibition in Petrograd (St Petersburg) called 0.10: The Last Futurist Exhibition, the painter Kazimir Malevich, born near Kyiv, unveiled a set of entirely abstract paintings he called Suprematist: brightly coloured, dynamic geometric shapes. In the top corner of the room he hung Black Square: a black square on a white ground, nothing more.

That position was no accident. In a Russian home the top corner of a room is where icons are displayed, and Malevich knew it; some visitors thought it blasphemy.1 The square became, for later artists, the "zero point of painting": reduce a picture any further and it stops being a picture.

Malevich made more than one version. The 1915 canvas, now in the State Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow, has aged badly. Years of neglect have left it crackled, scuffed and discoloured, and colours from underneath show through the cracks. In 2015 Tretyakov researchers who examined it under a microscope reported two earlier pictures beneath the black, a Cubo-Futurist composition and then a proto-Suprematist one, plus a handwritten inscription they read as a racist joke:2 "Battle of negroes in a dark cave". They linked it to an 1897 monochrome joke picture by the French humorist Alphonse Allais with a similar title. The founding icon of abstraction may answer an old racist gag.

Not everyone accepted the "discovery". The art historian Andréi Nakov pointed out that he had persuaded the museum to X-ray the painting in the mid-1990s and had published the underlying composition in 2007, and that neither the handwriting nor the content of the inscription had yet been identified.3 That is how art history works at its best: claims tested against earlier records and rival readings.

Malevich kept faith with his square. When Stalin's regime clamped down on the avant-garde, he returned to painting figures, but he signed his late figurative works with the Black Square.

concepts.title: Hilma af Klint: First, and Hidden
concepts.contentHtml:
For most of the twentieth century, the story of abstraction had a handful of founding fathers. Then a Swedish woman's paintings came out of storage. Hilma af Klint, born in Stockholm in 1862, graduated with honours from the city's Royal Academy of Fine Arts in 1887 and became a respected painter of skilful figurative works. In private she was deeply involved in spiritualism and Theosophy. She worked as a medium with a spiritual circle called The Five, who believed they received messages from "High Masters" on a higher plane of consciousness.

In 1906 af Klint began painting radically abstract pictures: bold, colourful and untethered from any recognisable references to the physical world.1 That was years before Kandinsky, Malevich or Piet Mondrian took similar steps. Her great cycle, The Paintings for the Temple (1906–15), grew out of her spiritual practice; she believed her guides had commissioned it. Its group The Ten Largest, large canvases painted in a few months in 1907,2 traces the stages of life from childhood to old age, with botanical shapes, snail-shell spirals and geometric forms that drift between the microscopic and the cosmic. She dreamed of hanging them in a spiral temple.

Then she hid them. Convinced the world was not yet ready, she rarely exhibited the abstract works and stipulated that her work should not be shown for twenty years following her death,3 which came in 1944. It was all but unseen until 1986, and the Guggenheim in New York later gave her the first major solo exhibition in the United States.

So who was first? It depends what "first" means. If it means the first to paint non-objective pictures, af Klint has the strongest claim we know of. If it means the first to launch abstraction into the world, through books, manifestos and exhibitions that other artists saw and answered, Kandinsky and Malevich still matter more, because almost nobody saw her work. Her case also shows how the record gets made: what survives, what is shown and who is written into textbooks decides who counts as a pioneer.

title: The Urinal That Changed Everything
description: Duchamp's Fountain: the rejected entry, the lost original, the readymade idea and who really sent it

concepts.title: R. Mutt, 1917
concepts.contentHtml:
In April 1917 the new Society of Independent Artists opened a huge exhibition at the Grand Central Palace in New York. Its rule was radical: there was no jury. Anyone could join by paying a one-dollar initiation fee and five dollars in annual dues, and every member could exhibit.1 The French artist Marcel Duchamp, then living in New York, was closely involved with the Society.

Just before the show opened, an entry arrived: a white porcelain urinal, an ordinary men's lavatory fitting, placed on its back and signed "R. Mutt 1917". Its title was Fountain. The committee refused to exhibit it, and Duchamp resigned in protest. The urinal never appeared in the show.2 Instead it was taken to the studio of the photographer Alfred Stieglitz to be photographed, and in May a small magazine run by Duchamp and two friends, The Blind Man, published an anonymous editorial in its defence: "Whether Mr Mutt with his own hands made the fountain or not has no importance. He CHOSE it.3"

Then the object vanished. The original Fountain is lost; what survives from 1917 is Stieglitz's photograph. Here is the twist most visitors never hear. The Fountains you can see today, at Tate Modern in London, the Centre Pompidou in Paris and elsewhere, are replicas made decades later. The Pompidou's, which it describes as the third version, was produced in 1964 by the Galleria Schwarz in Milan under Duchamp's supervision. It is not a shop-bought fitting at all, but white earthenware, glazed and painted, 63 by 48 by 35 centimetres. The most famous readymade in the world survives as a crafted object imitating a mass-produced one.

concepts.title: The Readymade: Art by Choosing
concepts.contentHtml:
Duchamp had a word for this kind of work: the readymade, a work of art made from a manufactured object. The term was itself borrowed, since by the end of the nineteenth century "ready-made" meant factory-made as opposed to handmade. His earliest examples included Bicycle Wheel (1913), a bicycle wheel mounted on a wooden stool, and In Advance of the Broken Arm (1915), an ordinary snow shovel inscribed with that title.

How did he choose? Deliberately without taste, he said. He picked ordinary, functional and rather dull objects, and explained in 1961 that his choice was "based on a reaction of visual indifference, with at the same time a total absence of good or bad taste". That is the real provocation. For centuries art had been judged by skill and beauty, and a readymade offers neither. This is why aesthetic definitions of art, which tie art to aesthetic experience, struggle with Duchamp; the philosopher Monroe Beardsley simply denied that the readymades were works of art.1

The Blind Man editorial packed the theory into three moves. First, choosing the object is itself a creative act. Second, cancelling its useful function changes what it is: nobody will use this urinal. Third, a new title and point of view create "a new thought for that object". The move from artist-as-maker to artist-as-chooser is often seen as the beginning of the road to2 conceptual art.

Was it a joke? Partly. Duchamp's circle loved puns, and in 1919 his friend Francis Picabia announced that Duchamp had gone to Buenos Aires to organise a hygienic service of urinals, "Rady-made". But the joke had a long fuse. In 2004, in the run-up to the Turner Prize, a poll of 500 art experts named3 Fountain the most influential work of modern art, ahead of Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and Andy Warhol's Marilyn Diptych.

concepts.title: Who Sent the Urinal?
concepts.contentHtml:
On 11 April 1917, two days after the urinal was rejected, Duchamp wrote to his sister Suzanne in Paris: "A female friend of mine, using a male pseudonym, Richard Mutt, submitted a porcelain urinal as a sculpture.1" He never named her. In 2002 Irene Gammel, biographer of the German poet and artist Baroness Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven, tentatively suggested the friend was the Baroness, partly because a journalist had reported that Mr Mutt lived in Philadelphia, as she did. Gammel's translation of the letter had the friend sending the urinal to Duchamp.

In 2014 the critic Julian Spalding and the scholar Glyn Thompson argued in The Art Newspaper that the Baroness was responsible. Their case: Duchamp wrote at the time that he did not submit it; the New York firm where he later said he bought it did not, they argue, stock that model; and its form and puns resemble God (about 1917), an inverted household plumbing trap mounted on a wooden mitre box. Yet the Philadelphia Museum of Art catalogues God under the painter Morton Schamberg: attribution is slippery even there. Spalding calls Fountain "the world's first great feminist, anti-war work of art".

Most Duchamp specialists disagree. The submission label carried the address of Duchamp's friend Louise Norton, a fact all sides accept. In 2019 the art historian Bradley Bailey published a text by Norton herself:2 "To test the bona fides of the hanging committee he sent in a porcelain urinal which he titled, Fountain by R. Mutt." On 19 April 1917 Stieglitz wrote to Georgia O'Keeffe that a young woman, "probably at Duchamp's instigation", had sent it. The shop argument rests largely on a Mott catalogue dated 1908.3 Thompson replies that the label is not in Norton's handwriting.

Weigh it yourself. For the Baroness: an ambiguous letter, a press report of a Philadelphia address, and a likeness to God. For Duchamp: Norton's own account, Stieglitz's letter and Picabia's joke. No document yet ties the Baroness directly to the urinal. The fight is fierce because, as one historian notes, nowhere is individual authorship more important than in the art world.

title: Drips, Fields and Spies: Abstract Expressionism
description: How New York painters made abstraction emotional, and what the evidence says about the CIA

concepts.title: Action Painting: Pollock on the Floor
concepts.contentHtml:
After the Second World War the centre of the art world moved across the Atlantic. By the 1950s it was generally accepted that the most exciting advances in painting were taking place in New York rather than Paris. The painters responsible, the Abstract Expressionists or New York School, made abstraction emotional. They took from the Surrealists the idea that art should come from the unconscious mind, and they fall into two broad groups: the action painters, who attacked their canvases with expressive gestures, and the colour field painters, who filled theirs with large areas of a single colour.

The most famous action painter was Jackson Pollock. He placed his canvas on the ground and moved around it, pouring paint from the can or trailing it from a brush or a stick.1 Look up Alchemy (1947), one of his earliest poured paintings, in the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice. It is about 1.1 metres high and 2.2 metres wide, made of oil, aluminium and alkyd enamel paint with sand, pebbles, fibres and broken wooden sticks on commercially printed fabric. Lines of paint thin, thicken, bleed and pool across the surface, topped with white paint squeezed straight from the tube. Here is a surprise: Pollock did not choose the title.2 His neighbours in East Hampton, Ralph Manheim and his wife, did. (The Fractals & Chaos topic covers studies of their fractal dimension.)

Was it art? Many Americans in the 1950s disliked modern art, and plenty of people still mutter that a child could do this. Yet in 1957, a year after Pollock was killed in a car crash at 44, the Metropolitan Museum in New York paid $30,000 for his painting Autumn Rhythm, an unprecedented sum for a painting by a contemporary artist at the time.3

Who were these painters? Not establishment figures. Pollock said that everyone at his Los Angeles high school thought he was a "rotten rebel from Russia". Mark Rothko said he was an anarchist, and Barnett Newman was a declared one. That matters later in this lesson.

concepts.title: Colour Fields and a Chapel
concepts.contentHtml:
The second branch of Abstract Expressionism was quieter. Mark Rothko, Barnett Newman and Clyfford Still were deeply interested in religion and myth, and built simple compositions from large areas of colour meant to produce a contemplative or meditative response in the viewer. Newman put the ambition plainly in 1948: "Instead of making cathedrals out of Christ, man, or 'life', we are making it out of ourselves, out of our own feelings."

The clearest test is the Rothko Chapel in Houston, Texas, commissioned by the collectors John and Dominique de Menil. It holds fourteen murals by Rothko: seven canvases with hard-edged black rectangles on a maroon ground and seven purple tonal paintings, lit by natural light that Rothko thought essential to show the subtleties of his colour. He completed them in 1967 and died in 1970, before he could see them installed. About 100,000 people of all faiths visit each year. Here a painting of almost nothing is asked to do what an altarpiece once did. And here is a surprise: Rothko steadfastly denied that his work was either Abstract Expressionist or Colour Field.1

Why should anyone call such pictures art, let alone great art? The strongest answer of the period came from formalism: the critical position that what matters most in a work of art is its form (colour, line, composition, the way it is made) rather than its story. Formalism reached its peak in the writing of the American critic Clement Greenberg, whose narrow theory of modernist painting made him hugely influential by the 1960s. In 1964 he organised an exhibition of thirty-one younger painters at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, titled2 Post-Painterly Abstraction. On the formalist view, the colour itself is the content, so a picture needs no subject. Lessons 6 and 7 show how that answer was challenged.

concepts.title: Did the CIA Make Abstract Expressionism?
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is a story that sounds like a conspiracy theory and is partly true. In 1947 the US State Department organised a touring exhibition, Advancing American Art, to rebut Soviet claims that America was a cultural desert.1 It caused outrage at home, one congressman called it "this kind of trash", and the tour had to be cancelled. The government could not openly promote modern art.

The CIA could do it quietly. In 1967 the New York Times revealed that the anti-Communist magazine Encounter had been indirectly funded by the agency, through the Congress for Cultural Freedom, set up with CIA funds in 1950 and active in 35 countries. The Congress sponsored exhibitions of the new American painting, and New York's Museum of Modern Art, whose president Nelson Rockefeller had close ties with US intelligence, was contracted to organise and curate most of its important art shows. When the Tate could not afford to bring The New American Painting to London in 1959, the money came through the Farfield Foundation, a secret conduit for CIA funds. A former CIA case officer, Donald Jameson, said in 1995 that such help was given at "two or three removes",2 under a policy of the long leash, so the artists never knew.

What does the evidence show? The art historian Irving Sandler, interviewed at 91, called the story untrue: "I haven't seen a single fact that indicates there was this kind of collusion",3 and he noted that the federal government at the time considered Abstract Expressionism a Communist plot. The curator David Anfam called the CIA's co-opting of the movement "a well-documented fact". Both can be partly right. The record shows CIA money helping to tour and celebrate the art abroad as proof of American freedom, set against Soviet Socialist Realism. It does not show the agency creating the movement, choosing what anyone painted or recruiting the artists, many of whom were ex-Communists. Even Frances Stonor Saunders, whose 1995 newspaper article and 1999 book made the case, judged that the movement would probably have dominated without this patronage.

title: Soup Cans and Brillo Boxes
description: Pop Art's raid on the supermarket, and the philosophers it forced to rethink what art is

concepts.title: Pop: Art from the Supermarket
concepts.contentHtml:
By the late 1950s many young artists felt that what they were taught at art school and saw in museums had nothing to do with their lives. Pop Art, which emerged in Britain in the mid-1950s and in America later in the decade, turned instead to Hollywood films, advertising, product packaging, pop music and comic books. In 1957 the British artist Richard Hamilton listed its qualities in a letter to friends: "Popular (designed for a mass audience), Transient (short-term solution), Expendable (easily forgotten), Low cost, Mass produced, Young (aimed at youth), Witty, Sexy, Gimmicky, Glamorous, Big business".

In America, Pop was a deliberate turn away from Abstract Expressionism. Instead of loose brushwork and the artist's inner feelings, it offered recognisable images with hard edges and impersonal, mundane subjects. Modernist critics were horrified by the low subject matter.

The decisive show opened in Los Angeles on 9 July 1962 at the Ferus Gallery on La Cienega Boulevard. Andy Warhol, who had worked in New York as a successful commercial illustrator, showed thirty-two canvases, each a single red-and-white Campbell's soup can. It was Warhol's first solo fine-art show and the West Coast's first Pop Art exhibition.1 Five canvases sold for $100 each; the gallery's co-owner Irving Blum then bought them back so the set could stay together.2 They are now in MoMA in New York.

Was this art, or advertising? That was exactly the question. Warhol's subject was the most ordinary object in an American kitchen, painted with no visible emotion, repeated like a product line. In 1962 he adopted the commercial production technique of screenprinting to speed up copying his images.3 The machine-made look was the point, and it led straight to the philosophical puzzle of the next concept.

concepts.title: Brillo Boxes and the Indiscernible
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1964 Warhol filled the Stable Gallery in New York with about 400 large replicas of supermarket product boxes. The most famous copied the printed cartons in which Brillo soap pads were delivered to supermarkets. To the eye, Warhol's boxes were more or less indistinguishable from the real ones.1

Here is a twist. The real Brillo carton had been designed about three years earlier by James Harvey, a commercial artist who was also a second-generation Abstract Expressionist painter. When Harvey saw his design in the gallery, he laughed it off, but his own dealers sent out a press release that complained: "Andy is running away with my box." So the Pop artwork copied a package designed, in his day job, by a painter of the movement Pop was rejecting.

The philosopher Arthur Danto walked into that show and came out with the problem of his career. If Warhol's boxes look just like the cartons, why is one a work of art and the other packaging? In his 1964 essay "The Artworld" he put it sharply: "Never mind that the Brillo box may not be good, much less great art.2 But if it is, why not indiscernible Brillo boxes that are in the stockroom? Or has the whole distinction between art and reality broken down?"

His answer was that you cannot tell art from non-art by looking. The difference is invisible: a context of theory and history he called the artworld, "an atmosphere of art theory". The same argument works for Fountain. Two urinals that look alike are aesthetically indiscernible, so if one is beautiful the other must be too, and beauty cannot be what makes only one of them art.3 Danto later argued that after the Brillo show art had reached its ultimate expression: from then on it could look like anything, and no style would advance a single story.

concepts.title: Does the Artworld Decide? Dickie and His Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
Danto's word "artworld" was taken up by the philosopher George Dickie, who built the institutional theory of art on it (the Aesthetics topic introduces it alongside rival definitions). In an early version (1974), a work of art is an artefact on which some person or persons acting on behalf of the artworld have conferred the status of candidate for appreciation.1 In a later version from 1984, a work of art is an artefact of a kind created to be presented to an artworld public, and artist, public and artworld are each defined in terms of the others.

Notice how this differs from Danto. For Danto, art needs meaning and interpretation: a work is about something, takes a point of view on it, and needs an art-historical context to be read. For Dickie, art is a social status. Being a "candidate for appreciation" is a deliberately low bar, and it says nothing about whether the work is any good.

Try the theories on this topic's cases. The refusés of 1863 were rejected by the official art world, yet an emperor's decree gave them a public; artworlds, it seems, can be plural and rebuilt. Fountain was refused by a committee but became art as Stieglitz, The Blind Man and later museums presented it. Af Klint's hidden paintings are harder: made for a temple that was never built and an audience in the future, were they art in 1910, when almost nobody had seen them?

Critics have found real problems. Art created outside any institution seems possible, although the definition rules it out, and the artworld, like any institution, seems capable of error.2 The definition looks circular. And it fits other institutions too well: the philosopher David Davies notes that both the artworld and a "commerceworld" seem to fall under it.3 Keep that thought, because in the final lesson the market starts making decisions of its own.

title: Ideas, Bodies and a $6.2 Million Banana
description: Conceptual art, performance and the market: how today's art world answers 'why is this art?'

concepts.title: The Idea Is the Art
concepts.contentHtml:
If Fountain showed that an artist could choose rather than make, conceptual art asked whether an object was needed at all. It is art for which the idea behind the work is more important than the finished art object. The term usually refers to art made from the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s, although Henry Flynt of the Fluxus group was already calling his performance pieces "concept art" in 1961.

The movement's best-known statement came from the American artist Sol LeWitt in the magazine Artforum in 1967: "In conceptual art the idea or concept is the most important aspect of the work.1 When an artist uses a conceptual form of art, it means that all of the planning and decisions are made beforehand and the execution is a perfunctory affair." If the planning is the art, the making can be done by anyone.

Conceptual art can look like almost anything: a performance, a photograph, a page of text. In 1969 the dealer Seth Siegelaub organised an exhibition in New York titled2 January 1-31: 0 Objects, 0 Painters, 0 Sculptors. The artist Robert Barry made a work called All the things I know but of which I am not at the moment thinking – 1:36 PM; June 15, 1969. Try picturing that one. You cannot, which is the point: there is nothing to see, only something to think about. Such works seem to lack aesthetic properties altogether, which is why they trouble definitions of art based on beauty.

There was a politics in this. Many conceptual artists tried to bypass the increasingly commercialised art world by stressing thought processes and methods of production. They chose forms that do not produce a finished object, so that the work could not be easily bought and sold and did not need a formal gallery.3 Remember that ambition; the final concept shows what the market did with it.

concepts.title: The Body as Medium: Performance
concepts.contentHtml:
Performance art is made through actions performed by the artist or other participants, live or recorded, spontaneous or scripted. Its history is often traced back to Futurist productions and Dada cabarets of the 1910s, but the term only became widely used in the 1970s.1 Its appeal was liveness, physical movement and impermanence: a performance cannot hang on a wall or be sold like a painting.

In 1964, at Yamaichi Hall in Kyoto, Yoko Ono performed Cut Piece for the first time. She sat silently on stage wearing her best suit while the audience cut away pieces of her clothing.2 She performed it again that year at a farewell concert in Tokyo titled Strip Tease Show, explaining that to strip meant not to reveal to others but to "discover something hidden in humans". The same year she published Grapefruit, a book of more than 200 instructions, which anyone can complete, some physically and some only in the mind.

What is the artwork here? Not the cut cloth, and not the photographs, though both survive. The work is the event itself: the audience's choices, the risk, the stillness of a woman letting strangers decide how far to go. That makes performance a hard case for every theory in lesson 6.

Performance can also be endurance. From the early to mid-1980s Marina Abramović and her partner Ulay presented their Nightsea Crossing works, in which they sat silently and motionless for anywhere from several hours to sixteen days.3 In 1988 they spent almost three months walking towards each other from opposite ends of the Great Wall of China, and when they met they formally ended their relationship. In 2010 the Museum of Modern Art in New York opened a retrospective of her work. As the theorist Jonah Westerman put it in 2016, performance is "not (and never was) a medium" but a set of questions about how art relates to people.

concepts.title: The Banana and the Shredder
concepts.contentHtml:
Now the market. In 2019, at the stand of the Perrotin gallery at Art Basel Miami Beach, Maurizio Cattelan showed Comedian: a single banana attached to a wall with silver duct tape. He called it "a sincere commentary and a reflection on what we value". Three editions sold for $120,000 to $150,000, and one is now owned by the Guggenheim. A performance artist ate the banana at the fair.

On 20 November 2024 another edition came up at Sotheby's in New York, estimated at $1 million to $1.5 million. After a seven-minute bidding war it sold for a hammer price of $5.2 million, $6.2 million with fees,1 to the crypto entrepreneur Justin Sun, who vowed to eat the banana. Here is the myth to bust: he did not buy a special banana. Sotheby's took it from the fruit stand outside its own headquarters. The winner owns a certificate of authenticity and Cattelan's instructions for displaying the work.2 The banana is replaceable; the idea and its paperwork are the art, just as conceptual artists proposed, yet this idea sold for millions.

Banksy turned an auction into the artwork. In October 2018 his Girl with Balloon, a spray-painted girl reaching for a red heart-shaped balloon in an ornate frame, sold at Sotheby's in London for a winning bid of £1 million. At that moment a shredder hidden in the frame whirred to life, leaving half the canvas hanging from the frame in strips.3 The buyer kept it, and as Love is in the Bin it sold again in October 2021 for £18,582,000 including the buyer's premium, close to 20 times its pre-shredded price.

So, why is this art? There is no single answer, but you now have a toolkit: ask what rule it breaks, what idea it carries, who presents it and to whom, and what it does to the people who meet it. And keep price apart from value. A sale tells you what one buyer would pay, not what a work means.
